title: Toppled Nawaz Sharif flies home to face the music – and cries “political revenge”!
text: He was thrown out of office. Now he is back. Pakistan's ousted prime minister Nawaz Sharif returned home on Thursday to face trial in an explosive anti-corruption case he calls political revenge, but which opposition leaders have branded accountability for the rich and powerful. Sharif had been in London with his wife, who is undergoing cancer treatment. He is due in court on Friday over allegations tied to London properties the family owns, charges that could land the former premier in jail. His allies are crying foul. Sharif, who served as prime minister twice and was toppled in a military coup in 1999, has supporters who call the proceedings a political vendetta and hint at meddling by elements of the powerful army. Sharif, 67, blasted the process in an interview on Wednesday in London before flying home. This case in the National Accountability Bureau is highly bogus and fake, which doesn t have links to corruption, he told Geo TV, comparing the process to charges laid against him after General Pervez Musharraf seized power in 1999. There is no kickback or misappropriation of the national exchequer, he added. Bogus? The Supreme Court disqualified Sharif from office in July over unreported sources of annual income of about $10,000, a salary the former premier denies ever receiving. And the court went further, ordering the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) to investigate and conduct a trial into the Sharif family's wider finances, including those London properties. Yet Sharif still controls the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) party, which elected his close ally Shahid Khaqi Abbasi as prime minister after Sharif was disqualified. It's a family affair: also facing trial before the NAB court are Sharif's daughter Maryam and her husband, Muhammad Safdar. They have all pleaded not guilty.

title: Texas House rams through crackdown on 'sanctuary cities' after marathon fight!
text: It was a brutal, 16-hour showdown – and the Republicans won. The Republican-dominated Texas House of Representatives on Thursday approved a bill to punish so-called “sanctuary cities,” brushing aside furious criticism from Democrats that it could lead to unconstitutional racial profiling. The timing is no accident. Republican U.S. President Donald Trump has made combating illegal immigration a priority. Texas’ Republican leaders have eagerly embraced Trump’s calls to punish localities they believe are shielding immigrants in the country illegally. But will it survive? Any anti-sanctuary city measure faces a rocky road after a federal judge this week blocked Trump’s executive order seeking to withhold funds from local authorities that do not use their resources to advance federal immigration laws. On a party line vote after about 16 hours of emotional debate, the House passed the bill to punish local authorities who do not obey requests to cooperate with federal immigration authorities. The bill must still be reconciled with another bill approved by the Texas Senate. Republican Governor Greg Abbott has said he would sign such a measure into law. “This bill has no effect on illegal immigrants if they have not committed a crime or are hanging out with someone who has,” bill sponsor Republican Charlie Geren told the House. Under questioning, Geren admitted to lawmakers that there are no local authorities in Texas at present that he would consider a “sanctuary city.”

title: Trump tax cuts will make your dream home even harder to afford, experts warn!
text: Bad news for anyone hoping to buy a home. The U.S. tax overhaul as currently proposed will make housing LESS affordable, according to nearly half of the property market experts polled – and another third say it would do nothing to help. A decade after the crash that wiped more than a third off U.S. home values and triggered a deep global recession, the housing market has roared back. U.S. house prices are expected to climb next year and in 2019, faster than predicted just a few months ago and at more than double the rate of underlying consumer inflation and wages. That is a stark contrast to the outlook for Britain. The S&P/Case Shiller composite index of U.S. home prices in 20 metropolitan areas is expected to jump 5.1 percent next year and 4.2 percent in 2019. The real crisis? A chronic shortage of homes, pushing prices out of reach of new buyers – who tend to be young, not particularly well-paid and, if university-educated, already crushed under huge amounts of debt. And now President Donald Trump’s administration is piling on with an overhaul of the tax code, which analysts say could wreck any potential improvements in affordability. The Republican tax proposal allows interest payment deductions on mortgage debt up to $750,000, down from the current $1 million. The House of Representatives is set to vote on the tax bill on Tuesday afternoon, and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said his chamber would vote on Tuesday evening. The verdict is grim: twelve of 26 analysts who answered an extra question said the tax bill in its current form will probably make housing more expensive. Eight said it would do nothing. Only six expected it to improve affordability.

text: It sounds like a thriller, but it's real. Indonesian authorities have uncovered a group spreading hate speech and fake news online – one of many that they fear could tear apart national unity. Religious and ethnic tensions exploded in the capital, Jakarta, this year when city elections pitted an ethnic Chinese Christian governor, who was accused of insulting Islam, against a Muslim candidate.

title: Trump pushes risky gamble: kill Obamacare mandate in tax bill!
text: Is Trump about to blow up his own tax bill? U.S. President Donald Trump is pressing Republicans to change their tax-cut bill to include a repeal of the Obamacare mandate that requires individuals to buy health insurance or pay a fine, the House of Representatives’ top tax lawmaker said on Friday. House tax committee Chairman Kevin Brady said he has asked the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) to assess Trump’s suggestion and indicated some lawmakers were considering it. Others are alarmed. They warned that adding such a divisive provision would expose the tax bill to the same fierce opposition that doomed Republicans’ efforts in July to repeal the 2010 Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare. The act was former President Barack Obama’s biggest domestic achievement. It raised taxes on wealthier Americans to fund healthcare benefits for middle- and low-income people, extending coverage to millions of previously uninsured. Democrats have defended it for years from attacks by Republicans, who see it as Washington meddling in Americans’ healthcare. Since Trump took power in January, he has pressed hard to tear down much of Obama’s work. Yet so far he has not secured a single major legislative accomplishment in Congress – even though Republicans control both the House and the Senate. And he is not letting up. “The president feels very strongly about including this (the individual mandate repeal) at some step before the final process. He’s told me that twice by phone and once in person,” Brady told an event hosted by Politico. “No decisions have been made ... Importing healthcare into a tax reform debate has consequences,” Brady said. Trump floated the idea in a tweet earlier this week, saying it would be “great” to repeal the mandate “and use those savings for further tax cuts.” Some Republican senators, such as Tom Cotton and Rand Paul, also favor this idea.

title: Sick abroad? The survival guide every traveler needs!
text: Nothing ruins a vacation faster than getting sick – and when it happens in another country, it can be truly unsettling and even scary. So what should you do? Matthew Klapetzky, a registered nurse and the clinical director of Passport Health, the travel clinic at the University of Rochester School of Nursing, shares his essential tips for when illness strikes abroad. “The majority of minor health issues that international travelers contend with can easily be with a good kit,” Mr. Klapetzky said. It should include a medication such as Imodium, because diarrhea is the most common ailment among travelers from the United States – striking around half of them! “This happens when your body gets a stomach bug as a reaction to a natural bacteria of a given land, and though it’s not usually serious, it lasts two to four days and can be extremely dehydrating,” he said. What else is a must? Ibuprofen to fight fevers, muscle inflammation and joint pain; bandages in assorted sizes along with an antibiotic ointment such as Neosporin for cuts and wounds; oral rehydration supplements such as CeraLyte to replace electrolytes lost through sweating and diarrhea; blister pads; and fiber supplements to ease constipation, also common during travel. And if you have allergies, such as to tree nuts, don't leave home without an EpiPen. Twisted your ankle? Heat rash? Some other situation where you need to see a doctor? Don’t hesitate – use local care. “Remember that the doctors where you are in the world are used to treating ailments specific to that region, such as severe sunburn, which is common in the tropics, so they are going to be your best bet to treat such issues,” Mr. Klapetzky said.

title: DOJ deploys fewer election monitors despite widespread concerns
text: The 2013 weakening of the Voting Rights Act means that fewer election observers with full access will be stationed at polling places. Because of that 2013 decision, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) will deploy 500 election monitors to polling places in 28 states on Tuesday, November 8, 2016. That is several hundred fewer than in 2012, and they will have limited powers. The DOJ made the announcement on Monday amid increased concerns about voter intimidation and discrimination. “The bedrock of our democracy is the right to vote, and the Department of Justice works tirelessly to uphold that right not only on Election Day, but every day,” said Attorney General Loretta Lynch. “The department is deeply committed to the fair and unbiased application of our voting rights laws and we will work tirelessly to ensure that every eligible person that wants to do so is able to cast a ballot.” However, the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Shelby County, Alabama v. Holder, which struck down parts of the 1965 Voting Rights Act (VRA), means that this work will be reduced compared with previous years. The 500 personnel will be deployed in 67 jurisdictions across 28 states; in 2012 there were 780 monitors sent to 51 jurisdictions in 24 states. Not all of the DOJ officials will have the full powers of election “observers.” Earlier, on Oct. 24, 2016, inflatable figures directed voters at the Santa Clara County Registrar of Voters in San Jose, Calif.

title: Michigan Republican bill to protect animals would also make oral and anal sex between humans a felony
text: An anti-animal abuse bill recently passed the Michigan state Senate. Protecting animals has broad support. However, Republicans considered the bill insufficiently focused on humans. In keeping with their long record of damaging the measures they handle, Republicans inserted language into the bill that would make human-on-human oral and anal sex a felony punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Senate Bill (SB) 219, sponsored by Republican state Senator Rick Jones, could have been further amended to remove the language penalizing sodomy (oral and anal sex) with a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, but it has not been. This approach is outdated, yet it is being treated as acceptable. The legislation states that it is a felony to engage in the abominable and detestable crime against nature with mankind or with any animal. Most people would agree that sexual contact with a horse is inappropriate and that a person who does it should be separated from the rest of society for a time, but most Americans also agree that the government must not police what happens in private citizens' bedrooms. Law Newz reports that Jones maintains that the language he personally inserted in the bill is not intended in any way to target the gay community, but also maintains that removing the with mankind portion will undermine the bill. SB 219 was designed to be part of a larger package of bills known as Logan's Law. The law is designed to prevent individuals convicted of animal abuse, animal torture or bestiality from possessing an animal for five years, and during probation, in the hope that the individual will seek mental health treatment.
